text: hey everybody what did the angel of the Lord and Satan have in common both of them are figures who originated
in generic Divine roles that later became associated with specific named individuals largely because of textual
interpolation in other words largely because an editor somewhere along the way anciently altered the text and that altered text was later reinterpreted as
a reference to a specific individual and I've talked about this a handful of times in relation to the angel of the Lord where we have these stories of God
themselves interacting with Hagar in Genesis 16 with Abraham in Genesis 22 with Moses in Exodus 3 with Balaam and
Numbers 22 with Gideon and judges 6 with manoak and his wife in Judges 13 and then somewhere along the way somebody
wrote the word malach messenger in before the Divine name or before the word Elohim creating the construction
the angel of the Lord that later gets interpreted as a specific reference to a specific angel
and we see this practice of using this word malach or the word angel in other languages to obscure God's presence and
activity in other places for instance where God comes to kill Moses for not circumcising his son in Exodus 4. in the
targumim those are angels who come to do that where Eve says I have procreated or
begotten a man with Adonai in the masoretic texts in the targomine that becomes with a messenger an angel of the
Lord so this is a practice that we know ancient editors were engaged in we also have this interesting case of the story of David's census in second Samuel 24 1.
and in that text it says that Adonai themselves became angry with David and incited David to conduct a census so
here we have similarly problematic Behavior just like in Exodus 4 where God wants to kill Moses so the chronicler in their telling of
the story Alters the text but rather than puts malach in front of Adonai to create the construction malach Adonai
the chronicler replaces the name Adonai with the word Satan without the definite article so it's not
clear that this is a specific generic role and this creates a text that seems to refer to some Satan some Satan Who
incites David to conduct a census and in later generations that text would contribute to the personification the
individuation of this generic role of the adversary as a specific named individual and by the time we get to the
New Testament Satan is no longer a generic role but the personal name of a specific Divine entity I'm going to be
discussing this and a lot more about the development of the concept of Satan in my upcoming online class on Satan in the Bible and you can find more information
about that on my link tree
